extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of classical Euclidean geometry (secondary/early-university)
extracted.subtask_description: Classical Euclidean propositions, problems, definitions, and exercises for proving theorems about triangles, angles, parallels, and for performing straightedge-and-compass constructions (bisectors, perpendiculars, triangle construction, etc.). Useful for learning, practicing, or verifying Euclidean proofs and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop VI — Equal angles imply equal opposite sides
rubrics_metrics.description: If two angles (B, C) of a triangle be equal, the sides (AC, AB) opposite to them are also equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect (reductio) proof: assume the opposite sides unequal, cut off a segment equal to the other side, join and compare triangles leading to contradiction. Questions for examination and relation to converse proposition are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop VII — Two triangles on same base with one pair of equal conterminous sides have unequal other pair
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles (ACB, ADB) on the same base (AB) and on the same side of it have one pair of conterminous sides (AC, AD) equal, the other pair of conterminous sides (BC, BD) must be unequal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cases (vertices outside each other, one vertex inside the other, vertex on base). Uses isosceles triangle angle equalities and axioms about angle inequalities. Exercises: circle intersection consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop VIII — Triangle congruence (two sides and included base equal)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles (ABC, DEF) have two sides (AB, AC) of one respectively equal to two sides (DE, DF) of the other, and have also the base (BC) of one equal to the base (EF) of the other; then the two triangles shall be equal, and the angles of one shall be respectively equal to the angles of the other (those opposite the equal sides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superposition argument: apply one triangle to the other so corresponding points coincide; includes Philo's alternate proof. Identified as second case of congruence in the Elements; refer to earlier propositions and axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop IX — Problem: Bisect a given rectilineal angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction: On AB take point D, cut off AE equal to AD, join DE, construct equilateral triangle DEF on DE (remote from A), join AF; AF bisects angle BAC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration by congruent triangles (DAF and EAF). Corollary: AF is an axis of symmetry. Exercises include alternative proofs and perpendicularity results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop X — Problem: Bisect a given finite straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction: Upon AB describe equilateral triangle ACB. Bisect angle ACB by CD meeting AB at D; then AB is bisected at D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by congruence of triangles ACD and BCD. Exercises: bisect by circles, locus properties of points equidistant from A and B, and from lines AB, AC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XI — Problem: From a point in a line draw perpendicular to that line
rubrics_metrics.description: Given point C on AB, take D on AC, make CE equal to CD, construct equilateral triangle DFE on DE, join CF; then CF is perpendicular to AB at C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via congruent triangles DCF and ECF leading to right angles. Exercises include lozenge diagonals, alternate proofs, erecting perpendicular at an extremity, and locus questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XII — Problem: From a point not on a line draw perpendicular to the line
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction: Take point D on other side of AB, draw circle with center C radius CD meeting AB at F and G, bisect FG at H, join CH; CH is perpendicular to AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by congruence of triangles FHC and GHC. Exercises: circle intersection properties and triangle decomposition into isosceles parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XIII — Adjacent angles made by a line standing on another are right or sum to two right angles
rubrics_metrics.description: The adjacent angles (ABC, ABD) which one right line (AB) standing on another (CD) makes with it are either both right angles, or their sum is equal to two right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by constructing perpendicular and angle decomposition. Corollaries: sum of two supplemental angles is two right angles; bisectors relations; various angle arithmetic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XIV — If two lines on opposite sides at a point sum to two right angles they form one straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: If at a point (B) in a right line (BA) two other right lines (CB, BD) on opposite sides make the adjacent angles together equal to two right angles, these two right lines form one continuous line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assuming BD not continuation leads to impossible equality (a part equal to whole).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XV — Vertical angles are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: If two right lines (AB, CD) intersect, the opposite angles are equal (CEA = DEB, and BEC = AED).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses supplements (adjacent angle sums equal two right angles). Short justification: opposite angles have common supplement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XVI — An exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either remote interior angle
rubrics_metrics.description: If any side (BC) of a triangle (ABC) be produced, the exterior angle (ACD) is greater than either of the interior non-adjacent angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct midpoint of AC and appropriate equal segments, compare triangles to obtain inequalities; corollaries on angle sums and area equalities, and on non-meeting of certain lines. Exercises include proving without producing a side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XVII — Any two angles of a triangle are together less than two right angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two angles (B, C) of a triangle (ABC) are together less than two right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by extending a side and using Prop XVI; corollaries: every triangle has at least two acute angles; if two angles unequal the lesser must be acute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XVIII — Greater side opposite greater angle
rubrics_metrics.description: If in any triangle (ABC) one side (AC) be greater than another (AB), the angle opposite to the greater side is greater than the angle opposite to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by cutting off equal segment or by circle construction and comparing angles; exercises include alternative proofs and consequences for quadrilaterals and perpendicular positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XIX — Greater angle implies greater opposite side
rubrics_metrics.description: If one angle (B) of a triangle (ABC) be greater than another angle (C), the side (AC) opposite to the greater angle is greater than the side (AB) opposite to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by eliminating equality and less-than cases using earlier propositions. Exercises: direct proofs and various comparative results about segments and perpendiculars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XX — Sum of two sides greater than third
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of any two sides (BA, AC) of a triangle (ABC) is greater than the third (BC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by producing a side and constructing equal segment; alternative proof using bisector. Exercises: difference of two sides less than third, perimeter relations, medians, and polygonal inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXI — From a point within triangle, sum of segments to base endpoints less than sum of other two sides and angle contained greater
rubrics_metrics.description: If two lines (BD, CD) be drawn to a point (D) within a triangle from the extremities of its base (BC), their sum is less than the sum of the remaining sides (BA, CA), but they contain a greater angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-part proof using side productions and triangle inequalities. Exercises: sums from interior points vs perimeter, and polygonal line length comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXII — Problem: Construct triangle with three given sides
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct a triangle whose three sides shall be respectively equal to three given lines (A, B, C), where the sum of any two is greater than the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via laying off segments on a line and intersecting circles centered at endpoints. Dem: show circles intersect when triangle inequality holds; questions explore necessity of the inequality and non-intersection cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXIII — Problem: At a point on a given line make an angle equal to given angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given point A on AB and given angle DEF, construct triangle BAC whose sides in order equal ED, EF, FD; then BAC equals DEF, giving required angle at A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solution reduces angle construction to triangle construction; exercises include many triangle-construction variants (SAS, ASA, etc.) and locus problems about sums/differences of distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXIV — If two triangles have two pairs of equal sides but contained angles unequal, bases compare accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles (ABC, DEF) have two sides (AB, AC) of one respectively equal to two sides (DE, DF) of the other, but the contained angle (BAC) of one greater than the contained angle (EDF) of the other, the base of that which has the greater angle is greater than the base of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by constructing equal-angle auxiliary triangle and comparing resulting bases; includes alternative proofs using sums of sides and bisectors. Exercises: variations on the proof and angle comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXV — Converse: Larger base implies larger contained angle
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles (ABC, DEF) have two sides (AB, AC) of one respectively equal to two sides (DE, DF) of the other, but the base (BC) of one greater than the base (EF) of the other, the angle (A) contained by the sides of that which has the greater base is greater than the angle (D) contained by the sides of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction considering equality/less-than cases; alternative direct construction provided. Exercise: direct demonstration by cutting off part equal to EF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXVI — Triangle congruence by two angles and included/similarly-placed side
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles (ABC, DEF) have two angles (B, C) of one equal respectively to two angles (E, F) of the other, and a side of one equal to a side similarly placed with respect to the equal angles of the other, the triangles are equal in every respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two cases: side equal is either between the given equal angles or opposite; proofs use contradiction by supposing non-equality and applying earlier congruence propositions. Includes definition of locus and many exercises about bisectors, concurrency, and right-triangle congruence cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def i–vii — Definitions for parallel lines, parallelogram, diagonal, third diagonal, trapezium, projection, and angle names
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: i) parallel lines do not meet at finite distance when produced indefinitely; ii) parallelogram defined; iii) diagonal; iv) third diagonal; v) trapezium; vi) projection of a line; vii) classification of angles made by a transversal (interior, exterior, alternate, corresponding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the foundational definitions used in propositions about parallel lines and their consequences. They establish vocabulary and geometric relations used repeatedly in subsequent proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXVII — If a transversal makes equal alternate angles the lines are parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: If a right line (EF) intersecting two right lines (AB, CD) makes the alternate angles (AEF, EFD) equal to each other, these lines are parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using the triangle formed by intersection; alternative symmetry argument via 180° rotation about midpoint of EF. Exercises: consequences for triangle exterior/interior angle relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXVIII — Equality of certain exterior/interior or interior sums implies parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: If a transversal (EF) intersecting two right lines (AB, CD) makes the exterior angle (EGB) equal to its corresponding interior angle (GHD), or makes two interior angles (BGH, GHD) on the same side equal to two right angles, the two right lines are parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-part proof reduces to showing alternate angles equal; uses earlier propositions and angle-sum facts. Useful as a checklist for detecting parallelism from angle relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXIX — Consequences of parallels with a transversal
rubrics_metrics.description: If a right line (EF) intersect two parallel right lines (AB, CD), it makes: 1) alternate angles (AGH, GHD) equal; 2) the exterior angle (EGB) equal to the corresponding interior angle (GHD); 3) the two interior angles (BGH, GHD) on the same side equal to two right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: unequal alternate angles would force parallels to meet. Includes exercises on perpendiculars, bisectors and intercepted segments between parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXX — Two lines parallel to same line are parallel to each other
rubrics_metrics.description: If two right lines (AB, CD) be parallel to the same right line (EF), they are parallel to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via comparing corresponding angles made by a common secant; uses transitivity of parallelism and angle equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXXI — Problem: Through a point construct line parallel to given line
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction: Through given point C draw CD to any point D in AB, then make angle DCF equal to angle ADC; line CE is parallel to AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses angle-copying construction; exercises include constructing triangle from altitude and base angles, drawing lines making given angles (two solutions), and various parallel-placement constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXXII — Exterior angle equals sum of two interior opposite angles; sum of interior angles equals two right angles
rubrics_metrics.description: If any side (AB) of a triangle (ABC) be produced (to D), the external angle (CBD) is equal to the sum of the two internal non-adjacent angles (A, C), and the sum of the three internal angles is equal to two right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via drawing through the vertex a line parallel to the opposite side and using alternate angle equalities. This is the classic angle-sum result for triangles; exercises and consequences follow.
